item.title: Shoulder Literature — 2026-09-26
item.itunes:author: Eric R. Wagner, MD, MSc
item.description: Weekly Shoulder Surgery Literature Digest — 2026-09-26 Pulled from PubMed across JSES, JSES International, AJSM, JAAOS, Arthroscopy, JBJS Am, and Bone & Joint Journal. This digest covers 2026-09-19 to 2026-09-26. It is a deliberately short one: only 7 shoulder-specific clinical and translational articles qualified — JSES International (4), Arthroscopy (2), and JBJS Am (1). The reason is straightforward and worth stating up front: the 2026-09-22 digest ran only four days ago and swept an unusually heavy 24-article window, so most of what the seven journals posted this week had already been covered. Per protocol the window was widened to 14 days when the 7-day yield fell below 8, and the widening added zero further shoulder papers — every 14-day extra was either already covered on 2026-09-22 or was a knee/hip/foot item or an editorial commentary. This is a genuinely quiet week, not a missed sweep. What did arrive is heavily weighted toward reconstruction of the difficult shoulder — the malunited proximal humerus, the malunited scapula, the failed posterior stabilization — plus two technology papers on navigation and kinematics and two biomechanics papers. The most clinically sobering paper of the week is a Walter Reed natural-history series on traumatic posterior glenohumeral dislocation in young, high-demand patients. Thirty-three shoulders in a predominantly active-duty military cohort were followed after a confirmed posterior dislocation or subluxation event, and the failure rates are grim in both arms: 61% failed nonoperative management (usually by recurrent dislocation) and 53% failed after surgery, most often requiring revision. Nearly half the operative cohort ended up on permanent duty restriction or never returned to their occupation. Posterior instability in this population is not the benign counterpart of anterior instability, and these numbers belong in the preoperative conversation. The most immediately useful technical paper is a Groningen–Adelaide cadaveric feasibility study of 3D patient-specific cutting and reduction guides for corrective osteotomy of malunited proximal humerus fractures, including a novel humeral-head–tuberosity separation technique for severe malunions with disrupted anatomy. Seven planned osteotomies landed within a median 5.2° of planned rotation and 3.4° of planned valgus — under 10° deviation across the board. This is a feasibility study on Thiel-embalmed specimens, not a clinical series, but it puts a technically forbidding operation on a planned footing. The largest dataset of the week is a navigation study out of NYU using 19,054 navigated total shoulder arthroplasties across 871 surgeons on the Advita GPS platform, asking how faithfully the preoperative plan is actually executed in augmented glenoids. item.title: Shoulder Literature — 2026-09-22
item.itunes:author: Eric R. Wagner, MD, MSc
item.description: Weekly Shoulder Surgery Literature Digest — 2026-09-22 Pulled from PubMed across JSES, JSES International, AJSM, JAAOS, Arthroscopy, JBJS Am, and Bone & Joint Journal. This digest covers 2026-09-12 to 2026-09-22. The window was set to close the gap since the 2026-09-13 digest, and it is a heavy one: 24 shoulder-specific clinical and translational articles qualified — Arthroscopy (8), JSES International (7), JSES (6), JBJS Am (2), and AJSM (1). The single most practice-changing paper is a Level I randomized controlled trial from Geneva and Lausanne. Eighty-six patients undergoing an open Latarjet were randomized to immediate self-rehabilitation with or without three weeks of sling immobilization. At six months the two groups were indistinguishable on every outcome, including graft union and osteolysis — but at two years the no-sling group was 12.5 Rowe points and 7.9 SANE-instability points ahead, was half again as likely to reach a patient acceptable symptom state, and the only two recurrent dislocations in the trial happened in the sling group. The routine post-Latarjet sling now has to justify itself. Running a close second in practical consequence is a Kaiser Permanente registry analysis in the same journal. Across 13,901 primary shoulder arthroplasties, anatomic TSA performed with an Exactech Equinoxe device carried a 1.87-fold adjusted revision hazard versus other devices — a signal that persisted (HR 1.91) when restricted to the implants packaged in the non-conforming bags that triggered the 2024 recall. Notably, no such difference appeared in elective reverse TSA. Anyone carrying an Equinoxe anatomic in their practice population now has a number to counsel with. The rotator cuff dominates the rest of the week. The Duke-led international consensus effort — 97 surgeons from 15 countries — lands in three simultaneous Arthroscopy papers covering diagnosis and posterosuperior repair (Part I), subscapularis, augmentation and tendon transfer (Part II), and reverse arthroplasty, revision and rehabilitation (Part III). The most instructive results are the failures to agree: graft augmentation and superior capsular reconstruction produced 16 statements with no consensus at all in Part II, and Part III found no agreement on any surveillance protocol. On the technical side, a Sydney prospective cohort of 1,000 consecutive undersurface knotless repairs of partial-thickness tears reports a 1.4% retear rate with a visible learning curve flattening after roughly 200 cases; a Seoul deep-learning volumetric study shows that supraspinatus muscle volume recovery at one year tracks tendon healing and independently predicts lower retear odds (OR 0.49 per 10% volume gain); and a Strasbourg series finds that low pain at one month after cuff repair — predicted by an intact subscapularis, no preoperative analgesics, and lower baseline pain — marks a patient whose whole first year runs better by more than the MCID. item.title: Shoulder Literature — 2026-09-13
item.itunes:author: Eric R. Wagner, MD, MSc
item.description: Weekly Shoulder Surgery Literature Digest — 2026-09-13 Pulled from PubMed across JSES, JSES International, AJSM, JAAOS, Arthroscopy, JBJS Am, and Bone & Joint Journal. This digest covers 2026-09-06 to 2026-09-13. It is a light week: 8 shoulder-specific clinical and translational articles qualified, split evenly between JSES (4) and Arthroscopy (4). Because the 7-day haul sat at the sparse threshold, the sweep was widened to 14 days (back to 2026-08-28); every shoulder article in the extra week had already been covered in the 2026-09-07 digest, so the widening added nothing new and is not double-counted here. The week's sharpest clinical message comes from Tampa. In a propensity-matched comparison of lateralized reverse shoulder arthroplasty with versus without a concomitant latissimus dorsi transfer, the transfer bought no additional external rotation and no better ASES improvement — but 96% of the transfer shoulders showed early proximal humeral osseous erosion against 4% of the reverse-alone shoulders. In the rotator cuff, a meta-analysis of five RCTs finds that leukocyte-poor PRP injected at the time of repair nearly halves the structural failure rate (15.9% vs 29.0%) yet moves no patient-reported outcome past its MCID; a Sydney study links shear-wave elastography stiffness to collagen disorganization and mixed cellularity on histology of the torn supraspinatus edge; and a 140,886-patient claims analysis ties alcohol use disorder to a roughly sixfold higher odds of 90-day adverse events after cuff repair, with pneumonia leading the list. Rounding out the week: a Seattle cohort finds that patient-reported allergies do not predict a poor anatomic TSA outcome on their own, but two or more allergies — and specifically allergies to medications other than antibiotics or analgesics — do; an HSS systematic review shows how inconsistently MCID, SCB, and PASS are derived and applied across 39 TSA studies; a Creighton biomechanics study shows a reinforced polyester patch sandwiched in a thin fascia lata graft brings SCR graft strength up to that of a thick graft; and a systematic review of 65 studies of shoulder surgery in contact and collision athletes finds return-to-play reporting too thin to compare across studies. JSES International, AJSM, JAAOS, JBJS Am, and Bone & Joint Journal published no new qualifying shoulder articles in this window. Letters, errata, author replies, editorials, and editorial commentaries were excluded, as were elbow-only, hand/wrist, hip, knee, foot/ankle, spine, and education/practice-management items. Search note: the window was swept by entry date (edat) and create date (crdt) across all seven journals with no keyword filter, and unioned; every record was screened by title and PMIDs were diffed against the 171 already covered in prior digests. item.title: Shoulder Literature — 2026-09-07
item.itunes:author: Eric R. Wagner, MD, MSc
item.description: Weekly Shoulder Surgery Literature Digest — 2026-09-07 Pulled from PubMed across JSES, JSES International, AJSM, JAAOS, Arthroscopy, JBJS Am, and Bone & Joint Journal. This digest covers a 10-day window (2026-08-29 to 2026-09-07) rather than the usual 7 days, because the scheduled Saturday 2026-09-05 run did not execute — the window was extended back to the day after the last digest so that no article fell through the gap. 18 shoulder-specific clinical and translational articles qualified, the largest haul in several weeks, and unusually Arthroscopy (8) outproduced JSES (6). The week's center of gravity is the rotator cuff, and specifically the question of what actually drives healing. A rat model from Xi'an defines a repair-tension "sweet zone" of 0.10–0.12 N/mm² with a bell-shaped relationship between tension and enthesis quality — the first quantitative answer to a question every surgeon settles by feel. A Chinese cohort shows early (<3 weeks) repair of traumatic massive tears beats delayed repair by 6.3 ASES points independent of confounders, while the retear rate stays stubbornly the same. A 5-year MRI series from Korea finds that superior capsular reconstruction grafts thin progressively even when they look intact, and that MR arthrography uncovers retear in 80% of symptomatic patients whom conventional MRI called healed. A systematic review out of Rush then decouples the outcome from the radiograph entirely: PROMs and forward flexion improve after cuff repair, SCR, and tendon transfer regardless of whether the acromiohumeral interval increases at all. On the arthroplasty side, two negative diagnostic papers land in the same issue and point the same direction: arthroscopic pre-revision tissue biopsy had 27–30% sensitivity for periprosthetic joint infection, and three patients with entirely negative biopsies grew ≥2 unexpected positive cultures at revision — a direct sequel to last week's 16S rRNA PCR paper from the same Wisconsin group. A meta-analysis of 2,639 patients finds single-shot interscalene block matches continuous catheters on 24-hour pain with a fourfold lower complication rate and a fraction of the cost. A Medicare analysis of 533,569 shoulder arthroplasties documents a 3.2-fold volume increase with surgeons still 88.9% urban and revision arthroplasty performed essentially nowhere but cities. And a 476,620-procedure UK linked-data study puts shoulder arthroplasty VTE at 1.0% — the lowest of the three major joints — with a 9% decline after the 2018 NICE guidance that hip and knee did not show. Rounding out the week: Hill-Sachs size tracks with dislocation-versus-subluxation rather than chronicity; distal radius allograft morphology varies enough by donor age and sex to matter for glenoid reconstruction; a deep learning model reads intraoperative arthroscopic images to predict retear; lag screws and wire cerclage beat suture-tape for allograft strut fixation; a rabbit model validates a new biceps tenodesis stitch; patient- and ph

item.title: Shoulder Literature — 2026-08-29
item.itunes:author: Eric R. Wagner, MD, MSc
item.description: Weekly Shoulder Surgery Literature Digest — 2026-08-29 Pulled from PubMed across JSES, JSES International, AJSM, JAAOS, Arthroscopy, JBJS Am, and Bone & Joint Journal over the last 7 days (2026-08-22 to 2026-08-29). A JSES-family week — 12 shoulder-specific clinical and translational articles, ten of them from JSES and JSES International. The headline pieces are a multicenter French Society of Shoulder and Elbow (SFEC) series of 209 chronic acromioclavicular reconstructions asking whether horizontal AC stabilization is worth adding, a 40,430-per-group TriNetX analysis linking hyperlipidemia to reoperation after arthroscopic rotator cuff repair (with the uncomfortable finding that statins did not help), a data-driven set of preoperative hemoglobin thresholds for total shoulder arthroplasty, and a Korean comparison of pectoralis major transfer versus subscapularis repair in reverse arthroplasty in which the transfer outperformed the repair on internal-rotation function. Two negative-but-useful diagnostic and implant papers round out the week: 16S rRNA PCR had zero true positives against ICM-confirmed shoulder periprosthetic joint infection, and short humeral stems were twice as likely to end up coronally malaligned as standard-length stems. AJSM, JAAOS, JBJS Am, and the Bone & Joint Journal each published no qualifying shoulder articles this week. Letters, errata, author replies, editorials, and editorial commentaries were excluded, as were elbow-only, hip, knee, spine, and wrist items. Search note: the 7-day entry-date window was cross-checked two ways — a create-date (crdt) sweep of all seven journals back to 2026-08-20, and a publication-date (dp) sweep with shoulder-girdle keywords — then diffed against every PMID covered in prior digests. Neither cross-check surfaced an additional includable shoulder article inside this week's window. The uncovered records they returned were all correctly excludable: a JAAOS radial head fracture technique series, a JBJS first-metatarsophalangeal measurement study, an AJSM revision-ACL analysis, an Arthroscopy all-inside meniscus device failure analysis, a JAAOS diabetes/HbA1c complication study, and four Arthroscopy editorial commentaries (mooring technique, tissue printing, hip labrum, dynamic anterior stabilization) plus the Bankart GLAD letter-and-reply exchange. --- Journal of Shoulder and Elbow Surgery (5) Hyperlipidemia Is Associated With an Increased Risk of Secondary Procedures in Patients Undergoing Arthroscopic Rotator Cuff Repair Prabhavalkar ON & Mannava S (corresponding author Prabhavalkar ON) — Department of Orthopedics, University of Rochester Medical Center, Rochester, NY, USA The largest and most clinically actionable paper of the week: a Level-III retrospective cohort using the TriNetX federated network of over 120 million de-identified records, asking whether hyperlipidemia — long suspected of impairing tendon-to-bone healing — actually translates into more reoperations after arthroscopic r

item.description: Weekly Shoulder Surgery Literature Digest — 2026-08-22 Pulled from PubMed across JSES, JSES International, AJSM, JAAOS, Arthroscopy, JBJS Am, and Bone & Joint Journal over the last 7 days (2026-08-15 to 2026-08-22). A solid arthroplasty-heavy week — 13 shoulder-specific clinical and translational articles, with JSES publishing a nine-paper batch that dominates the week and includes two randomized or registry-scale studies: an Australian National Joint Replacement Registry analysis of 63,502 reverse shoulder arthroplasties showing higher revision risk with non-crosslinked polyethylene, and a Level-I Turkish randomized trial finding that the immobilization device chosen for nonoperative proximal humerus fractures makes no difference to outcome. Also notable: a Norwegian minimum 5-year follow-up of the arthroscopic Latarjet in AJSM, the new AAOS Appropriate Use Criteria for mid-shaft clavicle fractures in JAAOS, and a Chinese arthroscopic "mooring" technique series for large anterior glenoid rim fractures in Arthroscopy. JSES International, JBJS Am, and the Bone & Joint Journal each published no qualifying shoulder articles this week. Letters, errata, author replies, editorials, and editorial commentaries were excluded, as were elbow-only items and articles already covered in earlier digests. Search note: the 7-day entry-date window was cross-checked against a publication-date sweep back to 2026-06-01 across all seven journals using shoulder-girdle keywords, then diffed against every PMID covered in prior digests. A moderate week — 12 shoulder-specific clinical and translational articles, with the JSES family again carrying the load (6 JSES, 3 JSES International) and headlined by a Rush propensity-matched comparison of anatomic arthroplasty with a posterior augmented glenoid against reverse arthroplasty for Walch B2/B3 disease, a Madrid matched-pair study of cement-augmented locking plates versus reverse arthroplasty for elderly proximal humerus fractures, and a Taiwanese randomized dose-response trial of extracorporeal shockwave therapy in adhesive capsulitis. A quieter week than the last — 13 shoulder-specific clinical and translational articles, concentrated almost entirely in the JSES family (7 JSES, 4 JSES International), and headlined by a Washington University randomized controlled trial on subscapularis repair in reverse arthroplasty. AJSM, Arthroscopy, and the Bone & Joint Journal each published no qualifying shoulder articles this week — their output was knee, hip, spine, trauma, and arthroplasty of the lower limb. Letters, errata, author replies, editorials, and editorial commentaries were excluded, as were elbow-only items and articles already covered in earlier digests. Search note: the 7-day entry-date window was cross-checked against a create-date sweep back to 2026-07-25 to catch back-dated ahead-of-print records. item.description: Weekly Shoulder Surgery Literature Digest — 2026-08-01 Pulled from PubMed across JSES, JSES International, AJSM, JAAOS, Arthroscopy, JBJS Am, and Bone & Joint Journal over the last 7 days (2026-07-25 to 2026-08-01). A strong week — 21 shoulder-specific clinical and translational articles, led by an eleven-article JSES batch. Letters, errata, author replies, and editorials/editorial commentaries were excluded, as were elbow-only and non-shoulder items and one AJSM article (the nerve-block network meta-analysis) already covered in last week's digest. --- American Journal of Sports Medicine (3) Suprascapular Nerve Release Improves the Histological Healing Morphology and Biomechanical Strength of the Rotator Cuff in a Rat Chronic Massive Rotator Cuff Tear Model Zhang W & Sun Y — Department of Hand Surgery, Affiliated Hospital of Nantong University, Nantong, China A controlled laboratory study in a rat chronic massive rotator cuff tear model (bilateral supraspinatus/infraspinatus transection, repaired at 4 weeks) asking whether suprascapular nerve entrapment is an independent barrier to tendon healing: neurofilament-200 staining showed entrapment in 7 of 10 shoulders, and adding concurrent nerve release to repair (n=14 rats per group) produced significantly higher maximum load at 8 weeks and better histologic healing scores at both 4 and 8 weeks — preclinical support for considering release at the time of massive cuff repair. PubMed Mid- to Long-term Outcomes of Coracoclavicular Ligament Reconstruction for Acromioclavicular Joint Dislocations: A Systematic Review of Studies With Minimum 5-Year Follow-up Boufadel P & Li X — Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Boston University School of Medicine, Boston, MA, USA A Level-IV systematic review of 16 studies (326 patients, 327 shoulders; weighted mean age 37 years, 85% men, mean follow-up 98 months) of open and arthroscopic coracoclavicular ligament reconstruction for Rockwood III–V acromioclavicular dislocations: functional results were excellent regardless of approach or technique (mean Constant 93.1, ASES 93.1, VAS 0.6), with 93% satisfaction and 88% return to preinjury sport, no loss of coracoclavicular distance over time, and overall complication, recurrence, and reoperation rates of 11.9%, 5.2%, and 6.1% — though arthroscopic procedures and suture-button/synthetic suspensory constructs carried higher recurrence and implant-related complication rates. item.itunes:author: Eric R. Wagner, MD, MSc
item.description: Weekly Shoulder Surgery Literature Digest — 2026-07-26 Pulled from PubMed across JSES, JSES International, AJSM, JAAOS, Arthroscopy, JBJS Am, and Bone & Joint Journal. Thin week — window widened to 14 days. The standard last-7-days pull surfaced only a handful of new shoulder items (below the ~8-article threshold), so per program rules the window was widened to 14 days (roughly 2026-07-12 to 2026-07-26). Most of what that widened window returned had already been covered in last week's (2026-07-18) sweeper digest — that run pulled the large JSES/JSES-International batch — and those duplicates were removed here. What remains is 4 genuinely new, non-duplicate, shoulder-specific clinical articles, one each in AJSM, Arthroscopy, JAAOS, and JBJS Am. Letters, errata, author replies, and editorials/editorial-commentaries were excluded (a JSES letter/reply on pharmacoepidemiologic real-world-data methods, a JSES editorial on the future growth of shoulder arthroplasty, and three Arthroscopy editorial commentaries — orthobiologics, stiff patients after cuff repair, and lower trapezius transfer), as were non-shoulder items (elbow — dynamic nerve MRI modeling, triceps-sparing total elbow arthroplasty, K-NOW unlinked total elbow kinematics; and the usual hip/knee/spine/foot content these general journals carry). --- American Journal of Sports Medicine (1) Nerve Blocks for Shoulder Arthroscopy: A Systematic Review of Randomized Controlled Trials With a Network Meta-analysis Hurley ET & Garrigues GE — Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Rush University Medical Center, Chicago, IL, USA A Level-I network meta-analysis of 63 RCTs (4,235 patients) comparing interscalene (ISB), suprascapular (SSB), and supraclavicular (SCB) blocks, combined block techniques, and general anesthesia alone for pain control after shoulder arthroscopy: interscalene block was the most consistent technique for reducing 24-hour opioid consumption (SUCRA 77.5%), while combined and alternative strategies (SCB+axillary at 2 h, SSB+costoclavicular at 6 h, SSB alone at 12 h) gave incremental pain-control advantages at specific early time points, with only modest separation from ISB by 24 hours.
